name: The Canopy
description:
Lake Forest was wealthy when wealth meant owning lakefront property. Now wealth means owning the jurisdiction the lakefront property exists in, and Lake Forest has adapted accordingly. The Canopy is a sovereign residential enclave — technically chartered under Axiom Industries' environmental governance subsidiary, practically governed by a homeowners' association with its own security force, its own courts, and its own definition of trespassing that includes 'existing within sensor range without authorization.' The name comes from the engineered tree canopy that covers the district: a bioengineered forest of modified oaks and elms that filter air, generate power through photovoltaic leaf coatings, and — not incidentally — block satellite and drone surveillance. Privacy, it turns out, is a natural resource if you can afford to engineer it.

The estates here belong to Tier 5 families — the executive class of the Big 20, legacy wealth dynasties that predate the sovereignty era, and the particular category of person who has enough money to live anywhere and chooses to live behind walls. The properties range from renovated historical mansions — some dating to the 1890s, maintained with the obsessive care of people who believe architecture is heritage — to new construction that looks like someone asked an AI to design a house for a person who has never experienced a consequence. The average lot size is four acres. The average property value is Φ180 million. The average occupancy is 2.3 people. The math of that is the point.

Corporate operations don't happen here — that's what downtown offices are for. But corporate decisions do. The Canopy's private dining rooms, estate libraries, and climate-controlled gardens are where the deals that shape M88's power structure are negotiated away from surveillance, documentation, and the inconvenience of witnesses. When the CEOs of competing corponations need to agree on something that would be illegal if it were recorded, they meet in Lake Forest. When a board member needs to disappear for a weekend while a scandal is managed, they come here. The Canopy is not where power lives. It's where power sleeps, which is more honest.

The service population — approximately 4,000 people who maintain the estates, operate the security systems, cook the meals, and raise the children of people who are too important to do it themselves — live in a carefully designed staff quarter on the western edge of the district. The staff quarter is clean, well-maintained, and completely separated from the residential zones by a sensor barrier that the residents call 'the garden wall' and the staff call 'the leash.'

sights: The engineered canopy — a continuous forest ceiling that filters sunlight into something golden and permanent, like a memory of weather that no longer exists
Estate gates set back from tree-lined roads, each entrance a statement of architectural philosophy and personal mythology
Security drones disguised as birds — convincing at a distance, unsettling up close
The lakefront bluffs, where the water below is somehow cleaner than anywhere else on the shore — because The Canopy's water treatment extends offshore
Staff vehicles moving along designated routes, never on the main residential roads
sounds: Silence — engineered, maintained, and enforced. The Canopy is the quietest place in the Corridor
Birdsong — real birds, attracted by the engineered canopy, supplemented by audio emitters when migration patterns disappoint
The faint hum of the perimeter security grid, audible only if you know what you're listening for
Wind through bioengineered leaves — a sound designed by acoustic botanists to be 'psychologically restorative'
Occasionally: children laughing. There are children here. They are well-fed and profoundly lonely.
smells: Clean air — genuinely clean, filtered through the photovoltaic canopy and supplemented by atmospheric processors
Old wood and estate gardens — the smell of maintained wealth, of things that are cared for because caring for them is someone's job
Lake breeze from the treated shoreline — what Lake Michigan would smell like if Lake Michigan had a budget
atmosphere.feel: A place that has solved every problem except the one that matters. The air is clean, the grounds are beautiful, the security is absolute, and the loneliness is architectural. The Canopy is designed to separate its residents from every form of discomfort, including the discomfort of encountering other human beings. It succeeds completely. The people here are the most powerful individuals in the Corridor. They are also the most insulated, which is not the same thing as the most protected, no matter how much they've paid to make it feel that way.

demographics: Approximately 8,000 residents, plus 4,000 service staff. Residents are exclusively Tier 5 — corporate executives, legacy wealth holders, and the small number of people whose net worth qualifies them for sovereign residential status. Staff are Tier 2-3, vetted through extensive background checks and neural loyalty screening. Average resident age: 58. Average staff tenure: 7 years, after which most are 'rotated' for 'security freshness,' which means fired before they learn too much.
economy: Wealth management, estate maintenance, and the informal economy of ultra-high-net-worth social networking. No commercial activity is permitted within The Canopy's boundaries. Everything is delivered. The economic output of The Canopy is measured not in production but in decisions — the agreements made in private rooms that redirect billions of Q in corporate spending.
power_structure: The Canopy Residents' Council — an elected body that functions like a corporate board for a municipality. Current chair rotates annually among the six founding families. Axiom's environmental governance charter provides the legal framework, but the Residents' Council holds effective authority. Security is provided by Sentinel Residential Services, a boutique firm that employs former Tier 3 Ringo and Axiom operators at salaries that ensure absolute loyalty.
dangers: Perimeter security — the automated defense grid treats unauthorized entry as a lethal threat, and it has the hardware to back that up
Social exposure — being seen in The Canopy without a reason to be there draws attention from people who can make problems disappear
Information asymmetry — The Canopy's residents know things about M88's power structure that outsiders don't, and they protect that knowledge aggressively
The staff quarter — entering through the service entrance is possible but requires credentials that are neurally verified and time-limited
Disappearance — people who cause problems in The Canopy don't get arrested. They stop existing in records.
opportunities: Intelligence — The Canopy is where M88's real decisions are made, and staff members occasionally talk
Blackmail material — the residents' personal lives are hidden behind the best security money can buy, which means the material behind that security is proportionally valuable
Service contracts — The Canopy's residents need things done that they can't ask their regular staff to do
The lakefront — The Canopy's treated shoreline is the only accessible clean water on the North Shore, and clean water has value
story_hooks: A Canopy resident — a Tessera board member — has requested a discreet meeting with someone from the Shelf, through intermediaries. The agenda is sealed. The urgency is real.
A former staff member, 'rotated' after nine years of service, has surfaced in the Circuit with a neural recording device that was never supposed to leave the estate grounds
The Canopy's perimeter security logged an intrusion that the system immediately reclassified as a false positive. The reclassification was manual. Someone inside authorized it.
frequented_by: Tier 5 corporate executives and legacy wealth holders
Service staff on restricted routes and schedules
Sentinel security personnel — visible at gates, invisible everywhere else
Fixers and operators, on rare occasions when a resident needs something the legitimate world cannot provide
